info.bio:
Roy Orbison nació el 23 de abril de 1936 en Vernon, Texas. Comenzó su carrera musical a finales de los años 50, tras fichar en 1956 por la discográfica Sun Records, con la que grabó su primer sencillo, "Ooby Dooby", un tema rockabilly con el que obtuvo unos discretos resultados. 

Aunque Roy Orbison comenzó como cantante country, pronto pasó al rockabilly. A pesar de ello, el estilo con el que brilló con luz propia fue el de las baladas. Su primer éxito como cantante de baladas fue el tema “Only The Lonely”, grabado en 1960.

scenes.name: Miami bass y 2 Live Crew
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: El grupo nació en la base aérea de March (California): David Hobbs (Mr. Mixx), que había visto a Afrika Islam scratchear y a la Rock Steady Crew bailar en Londres, conoció a Chris Wong Won (Fresh Kid Ice), luego uno de los pioneros asiático-americanos del rap; con Amazing Vee grabaron «The Revelation»/«2 Live» (1984) en Macola. La cara B nombraba a «Skyywalker», y Luther Campbell, DJ y promotor de Liberty City (un barrio negro partido por la I-95, como el Bronx por su autopista, y en llamas en 1980 tras la absolución de los policías que mataron a Arthur McDuffie), los llevó a Miami. Allí los Ghetto Style DJs y su Pac Jam en una pista de patinaje vivían para el bajo: «Planet Rock» y su 808 habían dado a luz el Miami bass (Maggotron, Pretty Tony, Amos Larkins y el «Bass Rock Express» de MC A.D.E., 1985). Con Brother Marquis y Campbell de maestro de ceremonias y dueño de Luke Skyywalker Records (Lucas le obligó a cambiar el nombre), grabaron «Throw the D» (1986), sobre «Dance to the Drummer’s Beat» y con trozos de Dolemite: el modelo del género, letras cada vez más explícitas y el argot de Miami («baby mama», «fuck boi»). El PMRC de Tipper Gore trajo la pegatina de Parental Advisory; la versión explícita vendía nueve veces más. En Nueva York los despreciaban como «’Bamas». «Me So Horny» (1989), con la frase de La chaqueta metálica y el «Firecracker» de Mass Production, llevó a As Nasty as They Wanna Be a los suburbios y al abogado Jack Thompson y al sheriff Nick Navarro a perseguirlo: en 1990 un juez federal lo declaró obsceno, detuvieron a un tendero y a Campbell y Fresh Kid Ice tras un concierto; con Henry Louis Gates de testigo («el juego de las docenas») el jurado los absolvió, la sentencia se anuló en 1992 y en 1994 el Supremo les dio la razón (9-0) en el caso de la parodia de «Oh, Pretty Woman». Fue el único disco de rap sureño de los ochenta en llegar al platino, y Campbell, el primer gran empresario del hip hop del Sur, mostró que no hacía falta un sello de Nueva York o Los Ángeles.

scenes.name: Antes del diluvio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: Early Career Struggle (1959)
podcast.body: By mid-1959, Roy Orbison was considered an "absolute failure" despite being produced by notable figures like Sam Phillips and Chet Atkins. He had been dropped by both Sun Records and RCA, and the money from his songwriting success for the Everly Brothers had run out. "By the middle of 1959, Roy Orbison was an absolute failure."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Personal Tragedies (1964-1968)
podcast.body: The period following 1964 was marked by severe personal tragedies for Roy Orbison. He divorced his wife Claudette in November 1964 due to her infidelity, though they reconciled and remarried in December 1965. Just six months later, in June 1966, Claudette died in a motorcycle accident. A little over two years after that, while Orbison was on tour in the UK, his house burned down, killing two of his three children. "The events of the next few years were the kind of thing that would break almost anyone."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: MGM Contract and Decline (1965)
podcast.body: Despite his continued success, Orbison's manager Wesley Rose, who had a strained relationship with Monument owner Fred Foster, moved Orbison to MGM Records. MGM offered him a substantial advance of a million dollars, but immediately after this move, his string of hits dried up. "Wesley Rose and Fred Foster had never got on, and Rose decided that he was going to move Orbison over to MGM Records, who gave him her advance of a million dollars, but immediately the hits dried up."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Wilderness Period (1965-1985)
podcast.body: For approximately 20 years, from 1965 to 1985, Orbison entered a "wilderness period." Plagued by personal tragedies, shifting musical tastes, and a heart condition developed in the 1970s, he struggled to produce records that resonated with the public. Compounding this, Monument Records went bankrupt in the 1970s, leading to his old hits being tied up in legal battles over ownership, making them difficult to access. "But for about 20 years, from 1965 through to 1985, he was in a wilderness period."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Posthumous Success (1989)
podcast.body: Roy Orbison died in December 1988 at the age of 52 from a heart attack, just as his career was experiencing a major resurgence. His new album, "Mystery Girl," released a couple of months later, soared to the top 5 or better globally. At one point, he had two albums simultaneously in the top 5 in both the UK (with a hits compilation) and the US (with The Traveling Wilburys album). "But by the time that came out, Orbison was dead."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Posthumous Hologram Tour (2018)
podcast.body: Despite having passed away in 1988, Roy Orbison embarked on a hologram tour in 2018. This tour, along with similar ventures for other deceased artists, showcased the advancements in projection technology that allowed lifelike 3D images to appear on stage, marking a new era for posthumous performances. "In 2018, Buddy Holly, dead since 1959, and Roy Orbison, dead since 1988, were on stage again as holograms."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Admired Guitar Skills
podcast.body: Sam Phillips was highly impressed by Orbison's guitar playing, often featuring him on other artists' records and claiming only Jerry Lee Lewis had a better sense of rhythm. Orbison's style mirrored Chuck Berry's, playing both rhythm and lead simultaneously, using bass strings for riffs and fills between vocal lines. "Rather oddly, given Orbison's later career, it wasn't primarily his singing that impressed Phillips, but rather his guitar playing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: B-Side Royalty Dispute
podcast.body: Billy Pat Ellis, drummer for The Teen Kings, co-wrote the rockabilly classic "Go Go Go" with Orbison, but was not credited on the label, leading to understandable anger and a dispute over royalties. "While Ellis had co-written the song, he wasn't credited on the label, which understandably caused him to get angry."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Band Influence for The Cramps
podcast.body: Roy Orbison was mentioned as an influence for The Cramps, alongside other rockabilly and early rock and roll artists, underscoring their embrace of primitive 1950s sounds. "También eran influencias para la banda Ricky Nelson, Roy Orbson, Jassie Latkins o Lingray."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Amor, Terror y Psychobilly: La Historia de The Cramps

podcast.title: Beatlemania Resistance
podcast.body: During the peak of Beatlemania in the UK and later the US, Roy Orbison was one of a very small number of American artists who continued to have hit records. In fact, two of his early collaborations with Bill Dees were the only two records by an American artist to reach number one in the UK between August 1963 and February 1965. "Indeed, two of the early collaborations by Orbison and Dees were the only two records by an American artist to go to number one in the UK between August 1963 and February 1965."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Commitment to Songwriting as Principal Art
podcast.body: While touring with Eddie Cochrane and Gene Vincent, Orbison noticed other artists struggling to find new material beyond their one hit. This inspired him to take his songwriting seriously as his primary artistic focus, ensuring a constant supply of new songs. "And he realised that the only way to ensure he would have a ready supply of new material was to write it himself, and so he started to take his songwriting seriously as his principal art."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Consistent Performance Style
podcast.body: Roy Orbison was not an improvisational artist; he meticulously planned and worked out his musical parts, adhering to them precisely in his performances and recordings. "Orbison was not a wild improviser, like many of the artists with whom Phillips worked. He would work out his parts exactly and stick to them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Devastation of Band Desertion
podcast.body: After "Rock House" failed, The Teen Kings, feeling neglected by Sam Phillips and overshadowed by Orbison, secretly packed their gear and left him during a recording session break. Orbison was devastated, feeling abandoned by friends he'd played with for years just as they began to find success. "He was absolutely devastated. The people he'd come up with as a teenager, the people he'd thought were his friends, had all deserted him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Discomfort with Stage Movement
podcast.body: Orbison and Melson's preference for through-composed songs also had a practical advantage for Orbison: their songs rarely had space for instrumental breaks. This meant Orbison did not have to engage in the typical rock and roll star performance of moving around and dancing while instrumentalists soloed, an activity he felt uncomfortable doing. Instead, he could remain perfectly still at the microphone and sing. "Instead, he could just stand perfectly still at the microphone and sing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Distinctive Artist of the Undocumented Era
podcast.body: Roy Orbison is noted as one of the few artists from the 1958-1964 period, alongside figures like Fabian and Frankie Avalon, who sometimes receives a slightly more subtle mention in historical summaries for having made "a decent record," highlighting him as an exception in an often-ignored era. "But there were some white red nun entities like Fabian and Frankie Avalon and also Roy Orbison and one or two others made a decent record."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 89: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow?" by the Shirelles

podcast.title: Early Musical Aspirations
podcast.body: Orbison grew up determined to be a singer. At age six, his father gave him a guitar and taught him "You Are My Sunshine," and by ten, he was already winning talent contests. "When he was six years old his father had bought him a guitar and taught him the chords to you are my sunshine and by the age of ten he was already winning talent contests."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: First Encounter with the Burnette Brothers
podcast.body: Roy Orbison first met the Burnette brothers in a Memphis radio station where he was chatting with Elvis Presley and waiting for a lift; when the lift doors opened, the Burnettes were inside, engaged in a fist fight. "The first time Roy Orbison met them he was standing in a Memphis radio station chatting with Elbas Presley and waiting for a lift."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 44: "Train Kept A-Rollin'", by Johnny Burnette and the Rock 'n' Roll Trio

podcast.title: Forfeiture of Songwriting Royalties
podcast.body: To leave Sun and allow The Everly Brothers to record his song "Claudette" (which was tied to Acuff Rose publishing), Orbison agreed to quit his contract with Sun by assigning all songwriting royalties for his previously recorded songs to Sam Phillips, a deal he resented for the rest of his life. "The deal he made was that Orbison quit his contract and signed with Acuff Rose, but only by signing all the songwriting royalties for the songs he'd already recorded, over to Phillips."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Inspiration from Lefty Frizel
podcast.body: Seeing country singer Lefty Frizel live was a pivotal moment for Orbison, not just for Frizel's vocal influence, but because seeing Frizel get into a Cadillac after a show made Orbison realize he could make real money from singing. "What really impressed young Roy Orbison though was seeing Frizel after the show getting into a Cadillac. Orbison realised you could make real money just from singing and started to make plans."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Joe Melson Collaboration Origin
podcast.body: The legend states that Roy Orbison began his pivotal songwriting collaboration with Joe Melson after Melson saw Orbison writing songs in his car. Orbison, having just had a son, Roy DeWayne Orbison (named after Duane Eddy), lived in a flat so small that he had to write in his car to avoid disturbing the baby. Melson tapped on the window, and upon hearing Orbison's explanation, suggested they work together. "Orbison and his wife Claudette had recently had a son, Roy DeWayne Orbison. His middle name was after Orbison's friend Dwayne Eddie, though spelled differently, and the flat they were living in was so small that the only way Orbison could write any songs without disturbing the baby was to go and write them in the car."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Joe Melson's Departure
podcast.body: Joe Melson, after several years of successful collaboration with Orbison, became increasingly convinced that he was the primary talent in their songwriting partnership. Melson also began releasing his own solo singles, culminating in his decision to stop working with Orbison after their last major collaboration, "Blue Bayou." "Melson was becoming increasingly convinced that he was the real talent in the partnership."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Johnny Cash's Unheeded Career Advice
podcast.body: Johnny Cash advised Orbison to sing in a lower register and consider changing his name for musical success, advice Orbison never took. Orbison would later joke with Cash about how poor this advice was. "He also advised Orbison that if he wanted to have any success as a musician he should probably start singing in a lower register and maybe change his name. Orbison never took that advice and in later years he would joke with Cash about how terrible his advice was."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Legacy as Tragic Figure
podcast.body: Roy Orbison's life is considered one of the saddest stories in rock music, marked by heartbreaking tragedies that derailed his career for decades. He died just as he was finally receiving the widespread recognition he deserved, leaving behind a body of work that continued to inspire artists long after his death. "Orbison is one of the saddest stories in rock music, with one of the greatest dance in its history getting derailed for decades by heartbreaking tragedies unimaginable to most of us."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Local Rock and Roller Rivalry
podcast.body: Roy Orbison, from Wink, Texas, was Buddy Holly's only serious local competition for the title of best rock and roller in their region, despite being a hundred miles away. "though he had an ongoing rivalry with Roy Orbison, who was from a hundred miles away in Wink, but was the only serious competition around for the best local rock and roller."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Overton Park Shell Concert (June 1)
podcast.body: Roy Orbison performed at the Overton Park Shell in Memphis on Friday, June 1, at 8 p.m., as part of a country rock and roll show. He shared the stage with Kyle Perkins, Johnny Cash, Warren Smith, and Eddie Bond and the Stumpers. "The new sensation Roy Orbison is team Kings with the Ubidubi."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2

podcast.title: Post-"Claudette" Upswing and RCA Deal
podcast.body: Following the success of The Everly Brothers' "Claudette," which sold half a million copies, Orbison received significant earnings, bought a Cadillac, moved to Nashville, and was quickly signed by RCA Records, who viewed him as "the next Elvis." "Roy bought a Cadillac, moved to Nashville, and quickly signed with RCA records, who saw in him the potential to be the next Elvis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: RCA Mismanagement and Career Setback
podcast.body: Despite being signed by RCA for his songwriting, Orbison was made to record material, often pop-country ballads chosen by Wesley Rose, that was not his preference and didn't suit his voice. His RCA singles performed worse than his Sun records, leading to him being dropped by the label after the money from "Claudette" ran out. "His RCA singles did even worse than his records on Sun, despite having the push of a major label behind him. Eventually the money from Claudette ran out, and he was dropped by RCA."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Recorded by Norman Petty
podcast.body: Norman Petty became interested in rockabilly after recording Roy Orbison and The Teen Kings' first single, "Ooby Dooby," which was quickly deleted. "Petty had become interested in rockabilly after having recorded Royal Bison and the team King's first single, the version of Ubidubi that was quickly deleted."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Return to West Texas
podcast.body: After being dropped by RCA, Orbison sold his Cadillac and moved back to West Texas. His career seemed over, and he faced the prospect of being remembered as a one-hit wonder. "Orbison sold his capillac and moved out of Nashville and back to West Texas. It looked like his career was over, and he would spend his life exactly as he'd hoped he wouldn't, as a musician who'd had one minor hit and never done anything else."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Rockabilly to Orchestrated Pop
podcast.body: After rockabilly music disappeared from the charts, Roy Orbison was one of the musicians who transitioned into performing "orchestrated pop." "all the musicians who had come up with Elvis had moved into orchestrated pop, like Roy Olberson."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 82: "Are You Lonesome Tonight?" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Role in "Class of 55" Album
podcast.body: Roy Orbison participated in the 1985 studio album "Class of 55," recorded at Sun Studios, where he filled in for the deceased Elvis Presley, joining Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins, and Jerry Lee Lewis. "4 years later, they would get together again, for a studio album recorded at Sun Studios, with Roy Orbison filling in for Elvis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Sam Phillips' Initial Rejection
podcast.body: When Orbison called Sam Phillips, as advised by Johnny Cash, Phillips' initial response was to tell Orbison to "tell Johnny Cash he doesn't run son records I do" before slamming the phone down. "Phillips responded by saying, tell Johnny Cash he doesn't run son records I do and slamming the phone down."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Signature Sunglasses Image
podcast.body: Orbison's iconic image of wearing dark sunglasses constantly originated by accident. While on tour with Patsy Cline promoting "Blue Angel," he left his regular glasses on a plane. Unable to see clearly without them, he wore his prescription sunglasses on stage and found that the audience perceived him as "cool and brooding," rather than "dorky" or "odd looking." From that point on, he adopted them as a permanent part of his image. "From that point on, he wore them constantly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Signing with Monument Records
podcast.body: Orbison's manager and publisher, Wesley Rose, introduced him to Fred Foster, the owner of the tiny, new Monument Records label. This move was surprising given Orbison's recent failures and Monument's lack of track record. "It seems odd that Roy Orbison could thank Wesley Rose for introducing him to monument records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Temporary Homelessness and Mentorship
podcast.body: Following The Teen Kings' departure, Orbison spent much of the next year effectively homeless, touring and staying with Sam Phillips, Johnny Cash, or Carl Perkins when in Memphis. Phillips, concerned for Orbison's well-being, invited him to stay in his home for several months and offered him profound life advice. "For much of the next year, Orbison was essentially homeless. He spent most of his time on tour, but considered Memphis his home base, and stayed with either Sam Phillips, Johnny Cash or Carl Perkins when he was at home."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Unique Relationship with Sam Phillips
podcast.body: Unlike other Sun artists who owed their careers to Phillips' discovery and molding, Orbison had been discovered elsewhere and initially rejected by Phillips. This meant Orbison never felt indebted to Phillips in the same way, creating a distinct dynamic. "That meant that Orbison would never feel as Elvis or Johnny Cash or Carl Perkins did, that he owed his career to Sam Phillips."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Unlikely Rock and Roll Star Persona
podcast.body: Roy Orbison made an unlikely rock and roll star; he was a quiet, unassuming man who, in his later years, wore dark glasses to conceal his face. His chosen music in later life, though rooted in rock and roll, was far from rebellious. "A quiet, unassuming man who rarely used a note stronger than mercy and wore dark glasses in later years to hide as much of his face as possible."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Unusual Song Structure Philosophy
podcast.body: Following the success of "Only the Lonely," Orbison and Joe Melson were convinced to follow their instincts and create songs with structures that deviated from the norm. They aimed for "through composed pieces" where a single melody developed with twists and turns, often without repeating sections, contrasting with the common verse-chorus-bridge structures of the time. "Instead, a single melody develops and takes twists and turns over the course of a couple of minutes, with Orbison usually singing throughout."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Vocal Isolation Booth Origin
podcast.body: During the recording of "Running Scared" (or possibly other early Orbison songs), a pioneering recording technique for Nashville was developed. Orbison's voice, though great, was not powerful enough to overcome the band and strings when recorded together in one room, leading to instruments bleeding into his vocal mic. To solve this, a coat rack covered with coats was brought into the studio and used to partition the space, with Orbison on one side and the band on the other. This makeshift isolation allowed his voice to be the primary sound on his mic, especially crucial for hitting a difficult high 'A' at the song's end. Chet Atkins was reportedly impressed enough to have RCA build a proper vocal isolation booth. "Eventually they brought a coat rack covered with coats into the studio, and used it to partition the space."

podcast.title: Voided Jewel Contract
podcast.body: After Orbison recorded "Ooby Dooby" for the independent label Jewel, Sam Phillips discovered Orbison was under 21, making the contract void. Phillips then signed Orbison to Sun and secured an injunction against Jewel to prevent further release of their version. "He discovered that Orbison wasn't yet 21 and so the contract he'd signed with Jewel was void. Phillips signed Orbison, got an injunction taken out against Jewel, preventing them from putting out any more copies of the single, only a few hundred ever got released, and quickly went into the studio to record a new version of the song."

podcast.title: Wesley Rose's Doubt
podcast.body: Despite Orbison's growing success with "Uptown," his manager Wesley Rose remained unsure that Orbison could ever be a star, primarily because he considered Orbison to be "odd looking." "Wesley Rose was still unsure that Orbison could ever be a star, mostly because he thought he was so odd looking."

xref.title: Posthumous Hologram Tour (2018)
xref.body: Despite having passed away in 1959, Buddy Holly embarked on a hologram tour in 2018. This tour, along with similar ventures for other deceased artists, showcased the advancements in projection technology that allowed lifelike 3D images to appear on stage, marking a new era for posthumous performances. "In 2018, Buddy Holly, dead since 1959, and Roy Orbison, dead since 1988, were on stage again as holograms."

xref.title: Early Home Recording Pioneer (1950s-1970s)
xref.body: Coming from a musical background, with his father Bob Moore playing on recordings for Elvis and Roy Orbison, R. Stevie Moore was inspired to make his own recordings at home. He utilized whatever gear he could assemble with his dad, including cheap cassette recorders or secondhand reel-to-reel machines, and began releasing records through his own label by the late 1950s. His work demonstrated an early embrace of home recording as a means of artistic expression. "R. Steve Moore was also in love with the cassette. The idea of being able to quickly record something on his reel to reel machine and then dub off copies onto cassettes for distribution was very appealing."

xref.title: Overton Park Shell Concert (June 1)
xref.body: Kyle Perkins, billed as "Mr. Blue Swade Shoes" and fresh from the Pericomo TV show, headlined a country rock and roll show at the Overton Park Shell in Memphis on Friday, June 1, at 8 p.m. He performed alongside other notable artists like Johnny Cash, Warren Smith, Roy Orbison, and Eddie Bond and the Stumpers. "Kyle Perkins will rock and roll in the Overton Park show for a great show Friday night, the first to June 8 p.m."
